items.explanation: The voyages were financed by ambitious monarchs like Ferdinand and Isabella and driven by profit, religious zeal, and better ships and instruments such as the caravel, astrolabe, and compass. Europe was not democratizing; royal power was growing stronger.
options: A. Pursuit of wealth and new markets
B. The spread of Christianity
C. The rise of democratic government in Europe
D. Advances in ships and navigation
items.stem: Which of the following did NOT help drive European expansion into the Western Hemisphere?

visual_adaptation.image_caption: Theodor de Bry, 'Columbus landing on Hispaniola,' 1594 — Spanish claim-taking in the Caribbean.
visual_adaptation.stem_addendum: The engraving above, Theodor de Bry's 1594 depiction of Columbus's landing on Hispaniola, illustrates the European expansion the question asks about.
visual_adaptation.key_check: Image depicts Spanish territorial claim-taking; key C (rise of democratic government did NOT drive expansion) is unaffected by the image.

items.explanation: The passage names two drains: the crown burned the surplus on the largest standing army in Europe and hegemonic wars against France, the Dutch, and England, while great landowners saw no reason to invest at home and preferred shipping raw wool to the Netherlands for finishing. Together, war spending plus elite hoarding explain why the windfall never became domestic development.
options: (A) American colonial governments kept nearly all colonial revenue through local taxation, sending little of it back to the crown.
(B) The crown poured the windfall into Europe's largest standing army and a string of hegemonic wars, while a small elite hoarded land and shipped raw wool abroad rather than investing at home.
(C) Dutch and English naval blockades cut Spain off from the trade networks it needed to commercialize its colonial wealth.
(D) The silver mines of Mexico and the Andes were largely exhausted within a generation, cutting off the flow of bullion to Spain.
items.stem: According to the passage, which of the following most directly explains why Spain's colonial wealth failed to produce domestic economic growth?
items.stimulus: The flood of gold and silver pulled from mines in Mexico and the Andes by coerced labor was a fortune Spain might have used to modernize its farms, workshops, and trade networks — to close the gap with the more advanced economies of northwestern Europe. Instead, Spain stayed in the grip of a small ruling elite of crown, clergy, and great landowners. In Castile, two or three percent of the people held ninety-seven percent of the land, and those great proprietors saw no reason to change: they preferred to run ever-larger flocks of sheep and ship the raw wool to the Netherlands for finishing. Meanwhile the crown poured the American windfall into the largest standing army in Europe, touching off an arms race and a string of hegemonic wars against France, the Dutch, and England. The deepest effect of all that circulating silver was a prolonged inflation that rippled across Western Europe. — adapted from A. Kent MacDougall's account of sixteenth-century Spain
items.pd_rationale: Woodcut of Potosi from Pedro Cieza de Leon, Cronica del Peru, 1553; pre-1930

visual_adaptation.image_caption: The silver mines of Potosi, woodcut from Cieza de Leon's Cronica del Peru, 1553.
visual_adaptation.stem_addendum: The 1553 woodcut above shows the silver mines of Potosi — the Andean bullion source described in the passage.
visual_adaptation.key_check: Image shows the bullion source Spain squandered; key B (wars and elite hoarding, not domestic investment) is unaffected.

items.explanation: Cortes's Second Letter (1520) was written to Charles V after Cortes defied his superior, Governor Velazquez of Cuba, to launch the Mexico expedition. Scenes of toppling 'idols' and preaching 'but one God' present a legally dubious private venture as faithful service to God and king -- exactly the framing Cortes needed to win retroactive royal approval.
options: A. Its portrayal of the expedition as loyal service to crown and church
B. Its scrupulous neutrality between Spanish and Aztec perspectives
C. Its criticism of the Spanish crown's colonial policies
D. Its argument that Native peoples should govern themselves
items.stem: The fact that this letter was addressed to Charles V best helps explain which feature of the document?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"In these chapels are the images or idols... the principal ones, in which the people have greatest faith and confidence, I precipitated from their pedestals, and cast them down the steps of the temple, purifying the chapels in which they had stood, as they were all polluted with human blood, shed in the sacrifices. In the places of these I put images of our Lady and the Saints... I answered, through the interpreters, that they were deceived in expecting any favors from idols, the work of their own hands... and that they must learn there was but one God, the universal Lord of all, who had created the heavens and earth, and all things else, and had made them and us."
—Hernando Cortés, Second Letter to Charles V, October 30, 1520 (abridged)
items.pd_rationale: Copy (1773, Manuel de Yllanez) of the c.1550s Lienzo de Tlaxcala; pre-1930

visual_adaptation.image_caption: Hernan Cortes introducing Christianity, from the Lienzo de Tlaxcala (c. 1550s; 1773 copy).
visual_adaptation.stem_addendum: The image above, from the Lienzo de Tlaxcala, shows Cortes introducing Christianity — the 'church' half of the loyal service to crown and church that the letter performs for its royal addressee.
visual_adaptation.key_check: Image supports the religious-service framing; key A (loyal service to crown and church) is unaffected.

items.explanation: In the first decades of contact, Native peoples did not quickly adopt European livestock. Horses and cattle spread gradually and were taken up widely only much later; the book notes Native peoples were initially terrified of the mounted Spaniards. Disease, missionary activity, and the transfer of American crops to Europe all began almost immediately.
options: A. Epidemics that devastated Native communities
B. The rapid adoption of horses and cattle by Native peoples
C. Missionary efforts to convert Native peoples to Catholicism
D. American crops such as maize and potatoes reaching Europe

items.stem: The conquest Prescott described was facilitated most decisively by
items.stimulus:
Questions 33–36 refer to the following excerpt.

The historian portrays Cortés as a daring and resourceful commander whose small Spanish force toppled the Aztec Empire through bold leadership, shrewd alliances with peoples subject to the Aztecs, and superior weaponry — while also recording the cruelty of the conquest.
—After William H. Prescott, History of the Conquest of Mexico, 1843 (paraphrased)
options: A. Spanish naval supremacy, Pacific bases, and maritime supply lines
B. Aztec alliances with the Portuguese and other European powers
C. Cortés's conversion to Protestantism and religious reforms
D. Epidemic disease, Indigenous allies, and Spanish weapons
items.explanation: Smallpox devastated Tenochtitlan, tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan and other allies fought alongside the Spanish, and steel, horses, and guns gave tactical edges.

visual_adaptation.stem_addendum: The Florentine Codex image above (c. 1585) shows smallpox victims — the epidemic-disease factor named in the keyed answer.
visual_adaptation.key_check: Image directly illustrates the disease component of key D (disease, Indigenous allies, weapons).

items.explanation: Las Casas's campaign against the brutality of the encomienda led to the New Laws of 1542, which restricted encomienda grants and the enslavement of Indians. In practice the crown's enforcement was weak, and Spanish colonists increasingly turned to enslaved African labor — a shift Las Casas himself first suggested and later recanted.
options: (A) New royal limits on the encomienda and a growing reliance on enslaved African labor.
(B) A royal decree abolishing slavery throughout the entire Spanish Empire.
(C) Spain's abandonment of silver mining in favor of subsistence farming in its colonies.
(D) The drawing of a formal boundary separating indigenous lands from Spanish settlement zones.
items.stem: In the 1540s, Spanish critics of forced indigenous labor — including the Dominican friar Bartolome de Las Casas — helped bring about which of the following changes?
items.pd_rationale: Theodor de Bry, 1598, illustrating Bartolome de Las Casas; Smithsonian American Art Museum, CC0

visual_adaptation.image_caption: Theodor de Bry engraving illustrating Las Casas's account of Spanish cruelty, 1598.
visual_adaptation.stem_addendum: The 1598 de Bry engraving above, illustrating Las Casas's denunciation of Spanish cruelty, shows the criticism that helped produce the New Laws.
visual_adaptation.key_check: Image supports the Las Casas context; key A (New Laws limiting encomienda; shift to African labor) is unaffected.

items.stimulus:
Questions 45–48 refer to the following excerpt.

"Squanto... was a special instrument sent of God for their good beyond their expectation. He directed them how to set their corn, where to take fish, and to procure other commodities, and was also their pilot to bring them to unknown places for their profit, and never left them till he died."
—William Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation (abridged)
options: A. The complete absence of Native-colonist contact
B. The total military dominance of the Pilgrims
C. The critical role of Native aid in colonial survival
D. Spanish missionary influence in New England
items.explanation: Bradford credits Squanto with teaching the Pilgrims to plant corn, fish, and navigate — aid without which the colony might not have survived.

visual_adaptation.image_caption: Jennie Augusta Brownscombe, 'The First Thanksgiving at Plymouth,' 1914.
visual_adaptation.stem_addendum: The 1914 painting above depicts the harvest feast symbolizing Native aid to the Pilgrims described in Bradford's account.
visual_adaptation.key_check: Image supports key C (critical role of Native aid in colonial survival).

items.explanation: Waldseemuller, working from Amerigo Vespucci's accounts, labeled the New World 'America' and drew it as landmasses separate from Asia — cartographic evidence that Europeans had begun to recognize a fourth, distinct continent rather than the eastern edge of Asia.
options: (A) Europeans had fully mapped the Pacific coastline of the Americas by 1507.
(B) The name 'America' honored the Spanish monarchs who financed transatlantic exploration.
(C) Europeans had come to recognize the lands across the Atlantic as a distinct continent rather than part of Asia.
(D) Waldseemuller's map was commissioned to fix the Treaty of Tordesillas boundary between Spain and Portugal.
items.origin_note: Original item authored in the visual-enrichment pass; not part of the 819 blind key audit.

visual_adaptation.image_caption: Martin Waldseemuller, Universalis Cosmographia, 1507 — the first map to name 'America.'
visual_adaptation.key_check: Author-verified: the map shows 'America' as separate landmasses; key C follows.

items.explanation: All four of Columbus's voyages (1492-1503) stayed within the Caribbean basin and the northern coasts of Central and South America; he never reached Asia, sailed for Spain rather than England, and died believing he had found islands off Asia.
options: (A) Columbus's voyages were sponsored by the English crown to challenge Spain's Atlantic trade.
(B) Columbus's landfalls remained concentrated in the Caribbean and along the northern coast of South America.
(C) Columbus reached the Asian mainland during his third voyage.
(D) Portuguese navigators retraced Columbus's routes to found colonies in Brazil.

items.explanation: Franciscan and later missionaries built the California missions to convert Native peoples to Catholicism and to anchor Spain's thinly held northern frontier with settled, loyal communities.
options: (A) Converting Native peoples to Catholicism while extending Spanish control over the frontier.
(B) Establishing self-governing towns modeled on English colonial charters.
(C) Building a plantation economy based on enslaved African labor.
(D) Training Native peoples for service in the Spanish navy.
